threat_assessment:
Two reads land on you before you untap on turn three, and both are wrong. Three players see a Howling Mine, a Temple Bell and Kwain handing out free cards, and file you as the friendly seat. The one player who has read about this commander files you as a storm deck sitting on Aetherflux Reservoir. Take the first read, spend it deliberately, and let the second one stay a rumour.

Because you are neither. You are a clock. An engine and a punisher come together in 56.7% of games and in 41.2% by turn six, mean turn 4.215 — that pair is your deck, so build every turn around reaching it. The four-card Reservoir kill assembles in 0.7% of games, 2.4% if you count the tutor, mean turn 6.809. Stop planning turns around a card combination you will meet once in a hundred and fifty games.

Now the rule that decides whether your generosity is clever or expensive. By turn six you have drawn a donation engine in 75.4% of games and a punisher in only 55.9% — the bands do not match, and the difference is a real slice of your games where you hold a Mine with nothing to charge for it. Do not cast that Mine. A donation engine with no punisher behind it is a gift the table gets to keep.

Say it as a sequencing law: punisher on board, or punisher in hand, before the firehose goes on. Scrawling Crawler is the one card that lets you skip the wait, because it hands out the cards and bills for them in the same permanent — lead with it whenever it is there. Everything else in the donation half waits for a partner.

Your library and your hand are both invisible. The table only assesses what you cast, so a Font of Mythos held for two turns costs you nothing and buys you two more turns of being nobody's problem.

Here is the turn you actually flip, and it is not the Reservoir. It is Iron Maiden joining a Mine that is already running: hand size minus four, on every opponent's upkeep, before they get to spend a single card you gave them. Stack 003 walks that upkeep and the damage is real. The turn that pairing goes public, stop adding to that side of the board and start holding mana — you own a clock now, and a clock wants counter mana, not more permanents.

Deflection is a budget and yours spends down every time the engine shows itself (strategy:multiplayer.threat-deflection). Three more moments spend it, so choose each one instead of stumbling into it.

Forced Fruition is the loudest permanent you own. Seven cards per spell, from every seat, and nothing about it reads as an apology once the punishers are down. Cast it after the table's removal is spent, never as your opening statement.

Heliod flipped with cards in hand is the second. He is available by turn six in 90.2% of games, so from that turn every untapped land you leave reads to the table as a counterspell — bank the misread. Leave two up on the turns you are holding nothing and let three players play around a card you do not have.

Aetherflux Reservoir standing next to Hullbreaker Horror is the third, and it is a confession. Anyone who has done the reading solves stack 006 on sight and points the pod's entire removal suite at your seat. Sol Ring and Arcane Signet are furniture and the Horror is a flash blocker with a bounce trigger, so deploy the Reservoir on the commit turn itself and never a turn early to develop.

Use Enlightened Tutor as a scheduler rather than a search. Fire it on the end step before your untap and your draw step delivers the piece, so the commit turn opens without the table ever seeing three of four on the battlefield. Early in the game it reads as value — a punisher, a tax piece, a doubler — and that is a version worth casting too.

When the storm turn does arrive, lead it with Grand Abolisher and lead the turn with him, not the turn before. A shield left standing through a full rotation is an announcement, and three players answer announcements at sorcery speed with three players' worth of mana. Led with, he closes every window for the rest of your turn and he is cast number one on the ledger.

Be exactly as honest about that turn as stack 006 is. Without the Abolisher, every loop cast and every activation hands priority to three opponents, and nothing in the engine closes any of it. Count the table's untapped mana before cast one, not after cast six (strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window).

Do not reach for Teferi's Protection as a combo shield. Your life total cannot change while it is up, so it cannot share a turn with a ledger that pays fifty life three times. Hold it for the swing back — it is the card that buys back the turn you spent becoming the archenemy, and that is the only job you should give it.

Drannith Magistrate carries political weight far past its two mana. Dropped into a fresh pod, it unites three commander-dependent players against you for nothing; dropped when one commander is already the table's shared problem, it earns you two defenders (strategy:multiplayer.politics). Sell it as the answer to their problem, and never promise anyone a lock — it stops casting, and that is all it stops.

There is one board where you should let the Reservoir show early. The punishers are already public, upkeeps are bleeding around the table, and you are holding free interaction, which you have by turn six in 67.2% of games. On that board the Reservoir soaks the artifact removal that would otherwise take Iron Maiden, and the fear it generates freezes a table already losing life for free.

Then set an expiry date on being nice. You have access to a win condition in 61.2% of games and in 50.5% by turn six, so treat the quiet phase as a phase and not a personality. The turn a punisher is charging and a closer is in hand, stop playing fair and take the game — you have already been paid for every card you gave away.
matchups:
One question sorts every table you sit at: can these three decks use the cards you are about to hand them? Answer it before the first Mine hits the battlefield. Your generosity is matchup-dependent; your punishers never are.

Against sweeper control and in the mirror, somebody has to be the beatdown and it is not you (strategy:whos-the-beatdown). Your clock advances while both of you pass — Iron Maiden and Ebony Owl Netsuke charge on their upkeeps whether or not you tapped a land — so refuse to spend first and let the upkeeps do the work. Keep Kwain untapped against the seat with open blue; a card you hand a control deck comes back as an answer.

Then take the reset they cannot counter. Supreme Verdict clears their board through open permission, and Jace Beleren, Jace Wielder of Mysteries, Teferi Temporal Pilgrim and Teferi Hero of Dominaria all live through it in both directions (strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math). Wrath freely — you are trading their creatures for none of yours.

Build your turns around Teferi, Hero of Dominaria here. The +1 draws and untaps two lands at the next end step, so the clock ticks while your counter mana stays up, and the −3 tucks the permanent they cannot rebuy. Take Archmage's Charm's draw-two mode in a standoff rather than sitting on a dead card.

The simulator puts 1.5 bodies on your board at turn six, so a creature wrath costs you almost nothing — keep it that way. Hullbreaker Horror is a combo piece, not a blocker. Flash him in as value against a control seat and the wrath that eats him costs you the kill, not a seven-drop.

Your real exposure is one artifact-and-enchantment sweeper taking the Mines, the punishers and the Reservoir in a single card. Deploy in layers and never show both halves to the same board state. A piece you have not fetched cannot be swept, so leave it in the library and let Enlightened Tutor collect it on an end step you choose.

Stax and taxes attack the thing this deck spends most turns doing: casting several cheap spells. Recount your hand under the tax before you sequence anything and assume the real number is one lower than it looks (strategy:threat-assessment.resource-denial). Under an assembling lock you are the beatdown, so decide fast.

Now the good news nobody expects from a control deck: your win condition does not tap. Iron Maiden, Ebony Owl Netsuke and Viseling charge on each opponent's upkeep with no mana from you at all, so under a Winter Orb-class lock you should be landing a punisher and settling in rather than trying to break out. Do not attempt to race a lock with the Reservoir kill — 0.7% of games, mean turn 6.809, and every cast in that turn is taxed.

Be more generous under a tax, not less. Heliod's back face cuts your costs by one for every card your opponents drew this turn, so tapping Kwain and running the Mines buys your turn back at a price the stax player cannot charge you for.

Answer the piece that beats you, not the first inconvenience. Teferi's −3 tucks a lock piece every other turn, Loran of the Third Path kills an artifact or enchantment on entry and again on every Displacer Kitten blink, and Cyclonic Rift resets a board of taxes at instant speed. Remember you are half a prison deck yourself — Drannith Magistrate turns off every seat that leans on its commander.

One caution when the mana gets tight: you run 31 blue sources against a 36 target, and Archmage's Charm wants three of them. Under a land tax or a colour-screwing lock, treat the Charm as a turn-four card and hold Swan Song or An Offer You Can't Refuse as your cheap answer instead.

Aggro is where your gifts can kill you, because an aggressive deck empties its hand and your Mines refill it. Never lead with Forced Fruition into that pod. Land Iron Maiden or Ebony Owl Netsuke first so the refill arrives taxed — stack 003 walks exactly that: hands over the limit pay on the upkeep, before the cards get spent.

Make yourself the worst attack at the table. Propaganda charges {2} per creature swinging your way, and The Second Doctor's rider takes a whole combat step from anyone who accepts his card. One card blanking three attack plans is what virtual advantage looks like in multiplayer (strategy:card-advantage.virtual), so sell the draw to the widest board every end step.

Commit little and hold Supreme Verdict. With 1.5 bodies at turn six you are not blocking your way out of this — absorb, let them overextend, and let the punishers get paid the whole time.

Then forget the Reservoir in this matchup entirely. The verified ledger in stack 006 starts from 32 life and pays fifty three times; against a fast board that life is not going to be there. Take Kwain's free point, treat every point of chip damage as disruption of a plan you were not running anyway, and win on the upkeep clock.

Against combo, assign yourself the control role and mean it (strategy:whos-the-beatdown). Your kill lands in 0.7% of games, 2.4% with the tutor, at a mean of turn 6.809 — that is slower and rarer than a dedicated combo deck in this bracket, so stop imagining you are the racer and start holding up mana. You have free or cheap interaction in 78.1% of games and 67.2% by turn six, which is plenty if you spend it right.

Spend it only on the card that ends the game (strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy). Countering a ramp spell is how you die holding a Force of Negation, and every one-for-one you fire early is a gift to the two players who did not have to cast it.

Give a storm deck nothing. Kwain stays untapped, the Doctor's offer gets sold to the other two seats, and Forced Fruition stays in your hand — seven cards per spell is their dream turn and your obituary. Land Drannith Magistrate early against a command-zone or cast-from-exile line and let it eat the removal earmarked for something of yours.

Know Drannith's limit before you tap out. It stops casting from anywhere but hand, so it blanks flashback, escape and commander recasts, and it does nothing at all to a reanimation spell that puts a creature straight onto the battlefield.

Graveyard hate pointed at you barely registers — your own yard use is a delve spell and a Torrential Gearhulk target, so let a Rest in Peace resolve and spend the counter elsewhere. Pointing at their graveyard is the harder half: you answer artifacts, creatures, enchantments and lands, and nothing you own touches a graveyard. Counter the reanimation spell, because you will never get a second chance at what it returns.

Whatever seat you draw, the shape of the plan does not move. Hand out cards that cost them more than they cost you, price the gift with a punisher before you hand it out, and treat the storm kill as a bonus you noticed rather than a plan you waited for. You are the one collecting.
how_it_wins:
The table has you filed as the nice one. You handed out cards, you never attacked, you said "sure, take one" three times. Then Iron Maiden invoices them for every card you gave away, on their own upkeep, before they get to spend it.

That is the deck, and you should play it in that order. Ten cards make the whole table draw. Six cards charge for the resulting hand. Both halves are on the battlefield in 56.7% of games and 41.2% of games by turn six — so more than half your games are the clock game, and you play toward the clock. Practical version: when you are holding a punisher and a donation engine, land the punisher first or on the same turn. Never after. A Howling Mine that goes down naked is you paying three opponents rent.

Close with Approach of the Second Sun. You reach a win condition in 61.2% of games and 50.5% by turn six, which is the single most reliable ending this deck has — cast it once, let it slot seventh from the top, gain the 7, and set the redraw with Mystical Tutor when you can. Stack 002 walks the second cast and finds it survivable behind held countermagic. So keep one blue up for that turn instead of spending it on the scary-looking spell that isn't going to kill you.

And then the famous one. Hullbreaker Horror plus a cheap rock plus Aetherflux Reservoir is a verified three-opponent kill — stack 006 does the whole ledger — and you will assemble it in 0.7% of games, 2.4% if a tutor helps, 0.3% by turn six. Read that as a gift, not a plan. Do not hold a hand together waiting for it, do not mulligan toward it, and do not tap out hunting the fourth piece. When all four show up on the same turn with Grand Abolisher available, take it. Every other game, you are the punisher deck, and the punisher deck wins by being boring on schedule.

combo_lines.001:
The clause that decides this is "choose up to one." A modal triggered ability has its mode and its targets locked in when it is put on the stack, not when it resolves (CR 603.3c: "If a triggered ability is modal, its controller announces the mode choice when putting the ability on the stack"). At that moment the artifact whose casting caused the trigger is still a spell, and CR 110.1 is precise about the difference: "A permanent is a card or token on the battlefield." A spell on the stack is neither.

So the trigger cannot name the card that made it. Either no mode is chosen and the ability leaves the stack (CR 603.3c), or the mode bounces some other permanent, which does nothing repeatable.

The holding, plainly: the two-card line the combo database lists — infinite colourless mana, infinite storm count — does not exist. The pair produces one Sol Ring activation. Whatever else drives this deck's bracket floor, this line does not.
combo_lines.002:
The operative words are "you've cast another spell named Approach of the Second Sun this game." The condition tracks a casting event in the game's history. It does not track the card, which matters, because CR 400.7 says an object that changes zones "becomes a new object with no memory of, or relation to, its previous existence" — and the card did change zones when it went seventh from the top. The event survives what the object forgets.

The check happens during resolution, as an instruction the spell's controller follows in written order (CR 608.2c). It is not a state-based action, and CR 117.2e forecloses the remaining question: "no player has priority while a spell or ability is resolving."

That fixes the window exactly. Interaction lives while Approach is on the stack and nowhere after it. A counterspell there ends the matter; Swan Song answers a counterspell but, per CR 113.9, answers no ability. Once resolution begins, the game ends under CR 104.1 — "immediately when a player wins" — and the opposing life totals are never consulted.
combo_lines.003:
Rule 113.7a is the whole case: "Once activated or triggered, an ability exists on the stack independently of its source. Destruction or removal of the source after that time won't affect the ability." Forced Fruition's trigger goes on the stack above the spell that triggered it, so it resolves first (CR 608.1), and killing the enchantment afterwards does not claw the seven cards back.

Two smaller clauses do the arithmetic. Ebony Owl Netsuke carries an intervening "if" — seven or more cards — which CR 608.2a checks at both trigger and resolution. Iron Maiden carries none, and computes hand size minus 4 on resolution. Both belong to you while an opponent is the active player, so CR 101.4 puts the ordering in your hands, and here the order changes nothing.

Holding: 4 from the Netsuke and 3 from the Maiden against a seven-card hand, 7 damage in one upkeep, 18 down to 11. The cleanup trim at CR 514.1 still applies on this board — the record contains no walkthrough of what happens when a "no maximum hand size" effect deletes it.
combo_lines.004:
Again "permanent," and this time it works in your favour. When the second rock is cast, the first one is on the battlefield and is therefore a legal target under CR 110.1 — the targeting failure that refuted the two-card line does not recur, because the trigger names the OTHER artifact.

The ledger is what makes this a line rather than a curiosity. Three mana spent, three mana produced, per full cycle. Exactly neutral, not positive. CR 106.4 keeps the float alive across the cycle, and CR 732.2a permits the shortcut that makes the cast count arbitrarily large without playing it out.

Holding: the cast count is unbounded, the mana is not, and the engine on its own deals no damage and draws no cards. A note on the Medallions, since both are in the 99 and both are tempting: CR 202.2b provides that "objects with no colored mana symbols in their mana costs are colorless," and the glossary is blunt — colourless is not a colour. Neither rock is a blue spell or a white one. The discount applies to nothing here.
combo_lines.005:
Two clauses collide, and both are about timing. CR 115.1 fixes targets "as part of the process of putting the spell or ability on the stack," and they "can't be changed except by another spell or ability that explicitly says it can do so." CR 400.7 makes the blinked permanent a new object with no relation to the one that was targeted.

Together those foreclose the claim. Both triggers are announced against the board as it stands at the cast; whichever resolves first moves its object, and the second trigger's target is then illegal under CR 608.2b, or was never able to be the same object at all. There is no ordering in which both act usefully on one cast.

Holding: the cycle is not mana-positive and total mana is not unbounded. What survives is the engine of stack 004 — unbounded casts at zero net mana — plus a one-time kicker on the exit iteration, terminating with 3 mana floating. A payoff attached to this engine must key on cast count. Anything keying on mana has no basis in the record.
combo_lines.006:
"Pay 50 life" is a cost, and CR 119.4 governs it: a player may pay life "only if their life total is greater than or equal to the amount of the payment." That single sentence is why this kill is an arithmetic problem rather than a board problem.

The Reservoir's trigger reads "for each spell you've cast this turn," and CR 601.2i places the cast-trigger after the spell becomes cast — so cast n banks n life, and k casts bank k(k+1)/2. From 32 life, 15 casts is the proven minimum funding three activations; 14 fails, ending at −13. The walked line kills at 26, then 40, then 34 life, and leaves you at 2 with the loop still available.

The exposure is stated on the record and should not be softened. Activating is not casting, so Hullbreaker Horror never triggers during an activation (CR 117.1b), and CR 301.1 confines the loop's artifact casts to a moment when the stack is empty — meaning they cannot be made in response to anything. Every activation and every loop cast opens a fully open priority window that this engine does not defend.

Holding: on these cards alone the kill is complete. Three opponents at −24, −10 and −16 lose under CR 704.5a, and you win under CR 104.5 and CR 104.2a. Grand Abolisher is in the 99 and was not on this board; whether his static closes these particular windows is not something the record settles.

card_roles.Heliod, the Radiant Dawn // Heliod, the: Front face is a 4/4 that rebuys an enchantment from your graveyard; the back face is the reason you play him, granting flash to everything and cutting {1} off your spells for each card your opponents drew this turn. Transform when you can spend {3}{U/P} without giving up the turn — every Howling Mine trigger is three opposing draws and three mana off your bill.
card_roles.Aetherflux Reservoir: The ceiling. It gains you life per spell per turn and turns 50 of that life into 50 damage at any target, and stack 006 proves the full three-opponent kill off it. Deploy it as a life cushion in the normal game and take the kill only when the loop pieces arrive with it.
card_roles.Alhammarret's Archive: Doubles your draws and your life gain and nobody else's, which is the exact asymmetry this deck is short of. Play it into a board that already has a donation engine down, not before.
card_roles.An Offer You Can't Refuse: One mana to counter a noncreature spell, and the two Treasures you hand back cost you almost nothing in a game you intend to win on upkeep triggers. Use it on the commit turn, not on the first ramp spell you see.
card_roles.Approach of the Second Sun: Your most reliable ending. Cast it once for the 7 life and the seventh-from-the-top setup, then defend the second cast — stack 002 shows the only window opponents get is while it sits on the stack.
card_roles.Arcane Denial: Counter anything and let them draw two; you replace your own card at the next upkeep. Fire it freely, because two extra cards in an opponent's hand is exactly what Iron Maiden bills for.
card_roles.Arcane Signet: Two-mana fixing that produces either colour, and one of the two cheap rocks the verified loop runs on (stacks 004, 006). Cast it on turn two and remember it is a combo piece later.
card_roles.Azorius Signet: The second colour-fixing rock, and it filters generic mana into exactly the {W}{U} the double-pip spells want. Play it early; it is what makes a turn-four Teferi cast on turn four.
card_roles.Braingeyser: Point X cards at yourself for the fuel or at an opponent to shove their hand past Ebony Owl Netsuke's seven-card line before their upkeep. Save it for the turn a punisher is already down.
card_roles.Consecrated Sphinx: Two cards every time any opponent draws one, in a deck that makes all three opponents draw extra every turn. It will eat removal — hold interaction the turn you cast it, or cast it with the counter already up.
card_roles.Counterspell: Two blue, counter anything, no conditions. Spend it on the spell that ends the game or ends your engine, never on the flashy one.
card_roles.Cyclonic Rift: The reset. Overload it at the end of the turn before yours and take the board away from three players at once — this is also your answer to a stax board you cannot otherwise unstick.
card_roles.Dictate of Kruphix: Every player draws an extra card each draw step, and flash lets you land it at end of turn with counter mana still up. It is a donation engine — pair it with a punisher or you are just being generous.
card_roles.Dig Through Time: Delve makes it cheap in a deck that fills its own graveyard, and two cards from the top seven is how you find a punisher or the Approach. Cast it on a turn you were holding mana anyway.
card_roles.Displacer Kitten: Blinks one of your permanents on every noncreature cast — Sol Ring comes back untapped, Loran re-triggers, Mystic Remora returns fresh. Its infinite-mana reputation is refuted by stack 005, so play it for the value it obviously does.
card_roles.Dovin's Veto: Counters a noncreature spell and cannot be countered itself, which makes it your best answer to another blue deck's protection. Hold it for their commit turn.
card_roles.Drannith Magistrate: Shuts off every opponent cast that is not from hand — command zone, graveyard, exile, all of it. Deploy it against commander-reliant tables and expect to defend it.
card_roles.Ebony Owl Netsuke: Four damage to each opponent holding seven or more cards, on their own upkeep. Stack 003 confirms it checks seven both when it triggers and when it resolves — so fill their hand before their turn, not during it.
card_roles.Faerie Mastermind: Flash, flying, and a card every time an opponent draws their second in a turn, which in this deck is most turns. Its {3}{U} table-draw mode is a punisher enabler you can use at instant speed.
card_roles.Fierce Guardianship: Free counterspell while you control your commander — the single best card in your hand on the turn you tapped out. Cast Heliod before you tap low, so this stays live.
card_roles.Folio of Fancies: Deletes maximum hand size for everyone, which uncaps what Iron Maiden and Viseling charge, and its {X}{X} mode fills every hand at once. The mill mode is a real backup kill against one player.
card_roles.Font of Mythos: Two extra cards per player per draw step — the heaviest donation effect in the deck. Do not cast it without a punisher on the battlefield or already in hand.
card_roles.Force of Negation: Free on an opponent's turn if you pitch a blue card, which is how you protect an engine on the turn you had no mana. Keep a spare blue card in hand rather than emptying it.
card_roles.Forced Fruition: Every opponent spell hands its caster seven cards. That is enormous punisher fuel and it is also a real gift — stack 003 verifies the seven arrive even if they kill the enchantment in response, so land it when the punishers can convert it.
card_roles.Grand Abolisher: During your turn opponents cannot cast spells or activate abilities of artifacts, creatures or enchantments. That is the shield for your commit turn — deploy him the turn before, or lead with him.
card_roles.Howling Mine: Two mana, one extra card for everyone each draw step, and the cheapest way to start the donation half. It is a turn-two play only if you have the punisher to follow it.
card_roles.Hullbreaker Horror: Flash, uncounterable, and a bounce trigger on every spell you cast — and the one irreplaceable card in the verified kill. As a fair card it is a seven-mana wall that bounces a problem permanent every turn, which is most of what you will actually get from it.
card_roles.Iron Maiden: Hand size minus 4 to each opponent, on each opponent's upkeep, computed on resolution. Three mana for a clock that bills three players — this is the card the whole donation half exists to feed.
card_roles.Jace Beleren: The +2 draws for everyone, which feeds the punishers and Heliod's discount at once; the −1 draws you a card while the loyalty holds. Tick him up unless you specifically need the card now.
card_roles.Jace, Wielder of Mysteries: Draws while threatening to convert an empty library into a win, and he survives your own Supreme Verdict. Treat the empty-library win as an emergency exit, not a plan — nothing in the record walks it.
card_roles.Kami of the Crescent Moon: Two mana for an extra card per player per draw step. Cheapest donation engine on the curve, and a body the table has to decide whether to bother killing.
card_roles.Kwain, Itinerant Meddler: Taps to let each player draw and gain 1, which reads as a favour and is an upkeep bill. Use it every turn once a punisher is down, and skip it entirely when one is not.
card_roles.Leyline of Anticipation: Free on turn zero from your opening hand, and it makes everything you cast flash — which means every turn you spend holding counter mana can also deploy a threat.
card_roles.Long-Term Plans: The only unrestricted search in the deck, and the only card that can find Hullbreaker Horror. It puts the card third from the top, so cast it a turn or two before you need the piece.
card_roles.Loran of the Third Path: Destroys an artifact or enchantment on entry, taps to draw you and one opponent a card, and re-triggers on every Displacer Kitten blink. She is your most repeatable answer to a stax piece.
card_roles.Mathemagics: Draws 2^X, which is the biggest single hand-fill in the deck. Point it at an opponent with the punishers down and you are choosing exactly how much their upkeep costs.
card_roles.Metallurgic Summonings: An X/X Construct on every instant or sorcery you cast, which turns your draw-go turns into a board. It is how a permission deck stops being defenceless.
card_roles.Mystic Remora: One mana, and it draws off opposing noncreature spells unless they pay {4}. Play it early and let the cumulative upkeep kill it once it has drawn three or four — that is a fine trade.
card_roles.Mystical Tutor: Puts an instant or sorcery on top, which in practice means it fetches Approach of the Second Sun for the winning cast. Use it at end of turn so your draw step collects it.
card_roles.Path to Exile: One mana, exiles any creature, and the basic land they get is a price worth paying to answer a commander now. Keep it for the creature that actually kills you.
card_roles.Pearl Medallion: Cuts {1} off your white spells, which stacks with Heliod's per-draw discount on the turns the table is drawing. It discounts nothing colourless — the loop rocks are unaffected (stack 004).
card_roles.Propaganda: Every attacker costs {2} to send at you, and it blanks attack plans from three players for one card. Cast it before you need it, not after the board is wide.
card_roles.Prosperity: X cards for each player. Fill three hands in one shot, then let Iron Maiden and Ebony Owl Netsuke charge all three at their own upkeeps.
card_roles.Psychosis Crawler: Drains each opponent 1 per card you draw, and its size is your hand size. In a deck with draw doublers this is genuine reach — it just needs to survive a turn cycle.
card_roles.Rhystic Study: The tax everyone knows and nobody pays. Ask every time; the card is worth more than the awkwardness, and the {1} they pay is tempo you take anyway.
card_roles.Sapphire Medallion: Cuts {1} off your blue spells, and this deck is 61 blue pips across 40 cards, so it discounts almost everything you cast. It does not discount the colourless loop rocks (stack 004).
card_roles.Scrawling Crawler: Draws every player a card on your upkeep and drains each opponent 1 whenever they draw. It is a donation engine and a punisher in the same card, which is unusual enough to prioritise.
card_roles.Skyscribing: X cards for every player, plus a forecast mode that hands out one card a turn from your hand for {2}{U}. The forecast is the sleeper — it keeps hands topped up without you spending a card.
card_roles.Smothering Tithe: A Treasure every time an opponent draws and declines to pay {2}, in a deck that makes them draw constantly. Treat it as ramp: it is one of your 39 mana sources.
card_roles.Sol Ring: One mana, taps for two, and it is one of the cheap rocks the verified loop runs on. Cast it turn one every single time.
card_roles.Sphinx's Tutelage: Mills two per card you draw and repeats on a colour match, which in a deck this draw-dense is a real alternate clock on one opponent. Aim it at whoever you least want drawing.
card_roles.Stroke of Genius: Instant-speed X cards at any player. End of turn, point it at the opponent whose upkeep is next and they walk into the punishers holding a fresh hand.
card_roles.Supreme Verdict: Uncounterable board wipe, and your four planeswalkers survive it. Cast it when the table has overextended into your pillow effects, not the first time you are attacked.
card_roles.Swan Song: One mana to counter an enchantment, instant or sorcery; they get a 2/2 flier. It is your counter-to-the-counter on the turn you cast Approach of the Second Sun (stack 002).
card_roles.Swords to Plowshares: The cheapest creature answer in the game and the life they gain rarely matters against a deck that wins on upkeep triggers. Save it for a commander.
card_roles.Talisman of Progress: Two-mana rock that pays either colour for a point of life. It exists to make your turn-three double-pip spells cast on turn three.
card_roles.Teferi's Ageless Insight: Doubles every draw after the first in your draw step, which stacks with Alhammarret's Archive. It also doubles the triggers on Psychosis Crawler and Sphinx's Tutelage.
card_roles.Teferi's Protection: Your life total cannot change, you gain protection from everything, and your board phases out. Hold it for the turn a wipe or a lethal swing would otherwise end you — it is a whole turn of immunity.
card_roles.Teferi, Temporal Pilgrim: Gains loyalty on every card you draw, so he grows himself in this deck, and his −2 makes a Spirit that grows on every draw too. He lives through Supreme Verdict; deploy him into a board you intend to wipe.
card_roles.Temple Bell: Taps to draw the whole table a card. Cheap, colourless, and repeatable — ring it every turn once a punisher is down, and leave it untapped when one is not.
card_roles.The Second Doctor: Deletes maximum hand size for everyone and offers each player a card at your end step; anyone who accepts cannot attack you next turn. Every answer they give you profits you, which is the whole point of the card.
card_roles.Thought Vessel: Two-mana rock that also removes your own maximum hand size, so the X-draw spells you point at yourself are not wasted. It taps for colourless — it does not move your colour counts.
card_roles.Torrential Gearhulk: Flashes in and recasts an instant from your graveyard for free, which on a draw-go turn is a counterspell plus a 5/6. Cast it on an opponent's end step whenever you did not need your mana.
card_roles.Viseling: The same hand-size-minus-4 upkeep bill as Iron Maiden, on a body. It costs more, so it is the second punisher you deploy, not the first.
card_roles.Teferi, Hero of Dominaria: The +1 draws and untaps two lands at the next end step, so your clock advances without ever tapping out; the −3 tucks a problem permanent. In a slow game he is the best card in the deck.
card_roles.Archmage's Charm: Counter, draw two, or steal a one-mana permanent — never a dead card. It also wants {U}{U}{U}, the only triple pip in the deck, so cast it off duals rather than promising it on turn three.
card_roles.Enlightened Tutor: One white mana at instant speed for any artifact or enchantment, which here is Aetherflux Reservoir, a rock, a punisher, Rhystic Study or Smothering Tithe. It puts the card on top, so fetch a turn before you need it.
card_roles.Island: Fourteen copies, and the reason blue is castable at all. It is the land you fetch with Flooded Strand unless a double-white spell is the play.
card_roles.Plains: Three copies against 16 white pips. Keep one in play before you commit to a hand that needs double white.
card_roles.Adarkar Wastes: Untapped either colour for a point of life, or colourless for free. Take the damage on the turns that matter and the free mana on the ones that do not.
card_roles.Ancient Tomb: Two colourless for two life, which is how a four-mana commander lands on turn three. The life is real against aggro — it is not free.
card_roles.Command Tower: Untapped, either colour, no cost. The single best land in the deck.
card_roles.Deserted Beach: Untapped once you control two other lands, so it is a tapland on turns one and two and a dual afterwards. Play it early or not at all.
card_roles.Eiganjo, Seat of the Empire: A white source that can be discarded to shoot an attacking or blocking creature for 4, cheaper for each legendary creature you control. Free insurance in a land slot.
card_roles.Flooded Strand: Fetches a Plains or an Island for a life, which fixes your colour on the exact turn you know which one you need. Crack it in response to something, not on your own main phase.
card_roles.Glacial Fortress: Untapped if you already control a Plains or an Island, which after turn one is nearly always. Effectively a dual.
card_roles.Hallowed Fountain: Pay 2 life and it comes down untapped. Pay it — the tempo is worth more than the life in a deck holding counter mana.
card_roles.Irrigated Farmland: One of two lands that always enters tapped, and it cycles for {2} when you are flooded. Play it on a turn you were not going to spend all your mana.
card_roles.Mana Confluence: Any colour for a life, every turn. It is your cleanest answer to a hand that needs {U}{U}{U} or {W}{W} on the same turn.
card_roles.Mikokoro, Center of the Sea: A colourless land that draws the whole table a card for {2}. It is a donation engine hiding in the mana base — and a blank one until a punisher is down.
card_roles.Otawara, Soaring City: A blue source that channels from hand to bounce an artifact, creature, enchantment or planeswalker, cheaper for each legendary creature you control. Answers a problem permanent without spending a card slot.
card_roles.Prairie Stream: Untapped once you control two or more basic lands, which with 17 basics is usually true by turn three. Before that it is a tapland.
card_roles.Seachrome Coast: Untapped while you control two or fewer other lands — the mirror image of the rest of your conditional duals. Lead with it.
card_roles.Skycloud Expanse: Costs {1} to tap for {W}{U}, so it is a filter rather than a dual. Good on the turns you have spare mana, awkward on the turns you do not.
card_roles.Temple of Enlightenment: The other land that always enters tapped, and it scries 1 on the way in. Drop it on turn one or on a turn you are holding up nothing.

mulligan:
You keep 73.8% of opening sevens and average 0.329 mulligans, so the free first ship is cheap and you should use it without agonising. Keep two to five lands. Below two you are not casting anything on time; above five you are drawing lands in a deck that already hands you extras.

The keep you want is two or three lands, a mana rock, and one card that makes the table draw. Howling Mine, Font of Mythos, Kami of the Crescent Moon, Temple Bell, Kwain — any of them. That hand digs toward a punisher, and digging is the point: your turn-three land drop hits 86.6% of the time, so a two-land opener with a rock is a real hand, not a prayer.

Ship the mirror image. Iron Maiden, Ebony Owl Netsuke and Viseling with no donation engine is three blanks and a land — nobody's hand gets to seven cards on its own, and you will sit there holding a clock with nothing to wind it. One punisher plus one engine plus two lands is a snap keep. Two punishers and no engine is a mulligan even when the mana is perfect.

Mulligan to the class, not the card. There is no named card you are allowed to look for here — ten donation effects and six punishers exist so that you never have to. That goes double for the storm kill: it turns up in 0.7% of games at a mean turn of 6.809, so a hand is never a keep because it has Aetherflux Reservoir in it.

One more keep test: your commander lands on mean turn 4.133 and shows up by turn six in 90.2% of games, so you do not need him in the opener. A hand with white sources and no blue is the one to look hardest at — the deck's blue demand starts on turn one and Archmage's Charm wants three of them.
upgrades:
Ten cards, and six of them move a number the audit already flags. Start with the one that moves fastest: the punisher half is six cards, which is 36% of an opening seven. Black Vise makes it seven, and the corpus prices that step at 41%. One card, five points of consistency, one mana — that is the best exchange rate on the list.

Three cards chase a much smaller number for a much bigger prize. The verified kill assembles in 0.7% of games because its creature component holds exactly one card, and a named card is 7.1% of an opening seven. Tidespout Tyrant makes that component two. Teferi, Time Raveler offers Aetherflux Reservoir an engine that does not run through a seven-mana body at all, and Mana Vault is the rock whose ledger might differ from the pair stack 004 settled at exactly neutral. Lightning Greaves is the cheap version of the same worry — it does not raise the assembly rate, it just keeps the one creature alive.

Then the flat spots. Graveyard is one of five permanent classes and the only one no card in the 99 answers; Soul-Guide Lantern closes it for one mana without turning off your own Torrential Gearhulk. Blue sits at 31 sources against a 36 yardstick and white at 20 against 22, and Tundra is the rare card that moves both counts without adding to the tapland column. March of Otherworldly Light covers the three permanent classes your removal only answers on the way in.

The last two are about who your card advantage actually serves. Twenty-two copies of draw is double the floor, but a lot of it feeds four seats at once. Esper Sentinel only ever draws for you, and Windfall converts three no-maximum-hand-size effects into three refilled hands on a turn you pick — which is the difference between hoping the punishers hit big and scheduling it.

Four of the ten carry unsettled questions rather than settled ones. Mana Vault's arithmetic, Tidespout Tyrant's mandatory target, and the Teferi loop all want a stack scenario before anyone treats them as arithmetic. Worth knowing that going in.
mana_base:
Thirty-three lands across eighteen entries, and only two of them always enter tapped. Seven can enter tapped at all, and five of those are conditional — a shock you can pay through, or a dual that untaps itself once you control two other lands. Against a template that asks for 37-39, thirty-three is under, and the audit says so.

Except the land count is not the whole supply. Six rocks take it to 39 mana sources against a 37 target, so the deck is short on lands and at target on mana — and that is before a ritual and three cost-reducers that shrink the bills rather than pay them. You can see the gap in the goldfish: the turn-three land drop hits 86.6% of the time and the turn-six one only 47.1%, while mean available mana still climbs from 3.311 on turn three to 5.325 on turn six. The rocks are doing the second half of that job.

Now the interesting disagreement. Blue is 79.2% of the pips and 63.4% of the sources; white is 20.8% of the pips and 36.6% of the sources. That is 61 blue pips spread over 40 cards against 16 white pips over 14 — the deck is far bluer than its mana base is, and white is comfortably over-served. Blue lands at 26, lifting to 31 with rocks, against a 36 yardstick; white at 15, lifting to 20, against 22. Blue is five short, white two.

On-curve, that reads as 74.2% blue and 78.7% white off lands alone, and 83.9% and 88.1% once the rocks are counted. The 90% figure is a yardstick, not a possibility, in a 33-land deck — nobody gets there at this land count. The card that feels the five-source blue gap is Archmage's Charm, the only triple pip in the list, which is why it plays like a later card than its mana value suggests.

One quiet detail in the source list: Sol Ring and Thought Vessel produce colourless, so they add to the 39 sources and nothing to either colour count. Smothering Tithe does count for both, which makes the deck's best tax card also a piece of its mana base — a Treasure every time an opponent declines to pay {2}, in a deck built to make opponents draw.
